explains: A transition is an ARROW: a case leaving one place for another, because something happened and the conditions allowed it. Transitions are the verbs of the operational graph. Every one names the place it leaves, the place it arrives at, the event that fires it and the guards that had to hold — so a reader can trace any journey through any machine without opening a single source file. The lint refuses a transition whose places do not exist, and it refuses a machine with a place nothing can reach or a place nothing can leave.

fields.name: What to call the move in plain words — ideally the sentence a herald would say.
fields.flow: Which machine this arrow belongs to (data/flows.json).
fields.from: The place (or places) a case can be in for this arrow to fire. A list means the machine genuinely allows several origins, not that the author was unsure.
fields.to: The place the case arrives in. Always exactly one.
fields.on: The EVENT that fires it — the thing that happens. A transition with no event is a condition being re-checked, which is a different animal and is written as such.
fields.guards: The conditions that must hold (data/guards.json). An empty list means the arrow fires on the event alone, which is rare and worth noticing.
fields.cost: What the case pays to make this move — cohesion, fatigue, standing, willingness, coin. Free moves are marked so, because in this game most of them are not.
fields.explains: What this move means, and what it feels like when it happens to you.

transitions.name: The lines start forward
transitions.on: the first tick of the battle
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Deployment ends and the simulation begins. Nothing else in the game has this quality of a door closing behind you: every decision before this was reversible and none of them are now.

transitions.name: An army comes apart
transitions.cost: the losing army takes a further morale blow on top
transitions.explains: One side has stopped being an army. The battle phase ends and the pursuit begins, and the most important consequence is invisible unless you know to look for it: the command phase stops running. Every order you send from here is thrown into a hole.

transitions.name: The chase burns out
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Horses are blown, the light is going, and the runners have scattered into country nobody will follow them into. What was caught was caught.

transitions.name: Both sides break contact
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Somebody withdrew in good order and nobody chased. A perfectly respectable outcome that players routinely undervalue: you still have an army, and an army you still have next season is worth more than a field you held for an afternoon.

transitions.name: The day runs out
transitions.cost: both armies keep their fatigue and their dead
transitions.explains: A draw. Neither side broke, neither side left, and the light went. Both armies go home tired with nothing settled and every grudge that got them there still in place.

transitions.name: They begin to feel it
transitions.cost: the unit fights and moves slightly worse
transitions.explains: The first step down. Casualties, a friend breaking nearby, arrows they cannot answer — the accumulation shows, and the line thickens as men drift back into it.

transitions.name: The back ranks start to drift
transitions.cost: the unit is one bad moment from breaking
transitions.explains: Your last warning. The men at the back have already decided and the men at the front have not noticed. If a captain is going to shout, this is when.

transitions.name: They get a grip
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Back from the edge — a captain's exhortation, a threat removed, a friendly unit arriving. Note that it takes a real margin, not a single point: the unit must climb clear of wavering, not merely stop falling.

transitions.name: They are themselves again
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Fully recovered. Rare in the middle of a fight and usually the result of getting out of contact for a while — which is an argument for rotating a line that you can only act on if you kept a reserve.

transitions.name: They break
transitions.cost: all cohesion, the current order, and any posture — thrown away at once
transitions.explains: The unit stops being a unit. Note the origins: a STEADY unit can break outright without passing through the middle states, if enough happens at once — a flank charge into a fresh line does exactly that. This is the one arrow in the machine with no cushion on it at all.

transitions.name: They turn and stand
transitions.cost: the unit's one and only second chance
transitions.explains: Four conditions, all of which must hold at once, which is why rallying is uncommon and worth a great deal when it happens. The most controllable of the four is the last: a live captain near his men is the difference between a rout and a delay.

transitions.name: They re-form
transitions.cost: the second chance is now spent
transitions.explains: Back in the battle — as SHAKEN, never steady, and with nothing behind them. A rallied unit is a real asset and a fragile one, and the commander who forgets which is about to lose it permanently.

transitions.name: They are gone
transitions.on: running long enough with no rally left
transitions.cost: the unit, for the rest of the day
transitions.explains: Off the field. Most of these men are alive and will be counted alive in the aftermath — they are simply no use to you now. Losing a unit to flight rather than to death is much the better outcome next season and no comfort at all this afternoon.

transitions.name: They are destroyed where they stood
transitions.on: the strength check, before anything else in the machine
transitions.cost: the unit, permanently
transitions.explains: Checked first every tick, because a unit that no longer exists cannot be frightened. Reaching this from STEADY — killed in place without ever breaking — is the rarest and most honoured thing a unit can do, and the deed goes onto the record for the house to remember.

transitions.name: Set!
transitions.on: a brace order, or a standing plan firing on cavalry closing
transitions.cost: the unit must be stationary, and stays stationary
transitions.explains: Butts in the earth, points level. The single most valuable second in the game and one you very often do not have — which is exactly what standing plans are for. A plan that braces automatically when horses come inside a named distance is worth more than any order you could send by courier.

transitions.name: They come off the brace
transitions.on: the unit moving, or being ordered elsewhere
transitions.cost: all refusal, immediately
transitions.explains: Bracing is not a property, it is a posture, and it is gone the instant the unit steps. Every 'my spearmen got ridden down' story is this arrow firing one moment before the horses arrived.

transitions.name: Loose!
transitions.on: a shoot order, or a plan with a target in range
transitions.cost: ammunition, which does not come back
transitions.explains: Begin shooting. Every arrow is a real object out of a finite quiver, and a unit that is shooting is not bracing — which archers rediscover the moment horsemen appear on their flank.

transitions.name: Hold!
transitions.on: a cease order, running dry, or nothing left worth shooting at
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Stop shooting. Worth ordering deliberately rather than waiting for the quiver to empty, because ammunition spent on a target that was going to lose anyway is ammunition you do not have when the real threat arrives.

transitions.name: Stakes in
transitions.cost: a long stretch of doing nothing else
transitions.explains: Sharpened poles into the ground, angled at a horse's chest. Stakes refuse cavalry the way a braced line does, without getting tired and without pinning the men in place. The price is the time, and the time is the reason it usually does not happen.

transitions.name: They leave the stakes
transitions.on: the unit advancing off its position
transitions.cost: the stakes, which stay where they are
transitions.explains: Stakes do not travel. Advancing archers abandon everything that was protecting them, which is why a shooting line that wins its duel and then walks forward so often ends the day worse than one that stayed put.

transitions.name: They step off
transitions.cost: cohesion recovery stops
transitions.explains: Moving at last. Cheap in every currency, and the pace a well-handled army spends most of its day at.

transitions.name: They pick it up
transitions.cost: a little cohesion and fatigue
transitions.explains: The working pace of a battle: fast enough to matter, slow enough that the line survives the trip.

transitions.name: They run
transitions.on: an urgent order, or a plan firing
transitions.cost: real cohesion and real fatigue
transitions.explains: Hurrying. The fit men pull ahead of the tired ones and you arrive as a worse-organised version of what you set out as — which is a genuine trade, not a mistake, when arriving late is the bigger risk.

transitions.name: Charge!
transitions.on: a charge order, inside charging distance
transitions.cost: the most expensive move on the table, whether it lands or not
transitions.explains: The last hundred metres. Shock scales with the SQUARE of closing speed, so this is where battles are actually decided — and a charge that arrives at a braced line pays every one of those costs for nothing at all.

transitions.name: Halt
transitions.on: a halt order, reaching the objective, or contact
transitions.cost: none — and standing still is where cohesion comes back
transitions.explains: Stopping. Underrated as an order: a halted unit recovers its cohesion, and cohesion is what decides whether it can turn, hold and refuse.

transitions.name: They run the other way
transitions.cost: everything
transitions.explains: The nerve machine reaching across and taking the pace machine with it. Note that it fires from ANY pace, including a charge — a unit can break in the act of attacking, and men who break while charging are the ones who die in the greatest numbers.

transitions.name: The running stops
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Tied to the nerve machine's rally. The men stop, out of breath, and start finding each other again.

transitions.name: "At once."
transitions.on: the heed being computed, on arrival
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: What you are buying with every settled grudge and every season of wages paid on time. It never stops being worth it and it never becomes free.

transitions.name: "I'll see it done."
transitions.on: the heed being computed, on arrival
transitions.cost: you do not choose the method
transitions.explains: Compliance without conformity. He gets you the outcome by a route you did not pick — usually harmless, occasionally better than your idea, occasionally catastrophic in a way you will hear explained afterwards.

transitions.name: "Presently."
transitions.on: the heed being computed, on arrival
transitions.cost: the moment
transitions.explains: The cautious face of unwillingness. Nothing you can accuse him of — just enough delay that the opportunity has closed by the time the order is carried out.

transitions.name: "Some of us, then."
transitions.on: the heed being computed, on arrival
transitions.cost: half the contingent stays home
transitions.explains: The bolder face of the same unwillingness. He commits what he can afford to lose and keeps the rest, because he does not trust the order, or you, or the day.

transitions.name: "Follow me!"
transitions.on: the heed being computed, on arrival
transitions.cost: control
transitions.explains: The dangerous one, and the one that surprises players. A captain who does not respect you and has blood up does not sit still — he takes the largest possible reading of your order and your right wing goes with him.

transitions.name: A gesture, and nothing more
transitions.on: the heed being computed, on arrival
transitions.cost: the contingent, in all but name
transitions.explains: Hedging with contempt. Enough motion that he cannot be accused of refusing, and no commitment whatsoever. Functionally a defiance he can deny at the feast afterwards.

transitions.name: "No."
transitions.on: the heed being computed, on arrival
transitions.cost: the contingent, and the watching army's opinion of you
transitions.explains: Flat refusal in front of everyone. Nothing random put him here — and the herald names the largest cause out loud when it happens, which is the game telling you which of your decisions this was.

transitions.name: The courier goes
transitions.cost: one of your limited orders in flight
transitions.explains: Away he goes. How many you may have out at once is set by your Marshal — the court's most direct hand on the battle's controls.

transitions.name: He reaches the banner
transitions.cost: the time it took, which is the whole problem
transitions.explains: It got there. The distance you sent it across has already been paid in seconds, and in a battle seconds are the currency that matters.

transitions.name: He does not arrive
transitions.cost: the order, silently
transitions.explains: Killed on the way, and nobody tells you. From where you stand, an order that never arrived looks exactly like an order that was defied — and that ambiguity is deliberate, because it was true.

transitions.name: It becomes their job
transitions.on: the heed resolving to any form of compliance
transitions.cost: whatever the interpretation cost you
transitions.explains: Accepted in SOME form — which may not be the form you sent. From here it is the contingent's standing job until something ends it.

transitions.name: It is refused
transitions.cost: the order, and a great deal of face
transitions.explains: The captain will not do it. The contingent falls back on its standing charge and carries on with whatever it was already doing.

transitions.name: It is carried out
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Done. The contingent reverts to its standing charge and waits for your next idea.

transitions.name: It stops mattering
transitions.on: a newer order arriving, the target being gone, or the unit breaking
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Overtaken by events. Not a failure so much as a fact — and a reminder that an order you sent ninety seconds ago was aimed at a battle that no longer exists.

transitions.name: Something changes in them
transitions.on: the treachery reading crossing its first line
transitions.cost: nothing yet, which is the trap
transitions.explains: Nothing has happened. The number moved, and the number is public if you go and look at it — the forecast will tell you before the battle. Almost nobody looks.

transitions.name: They start working against you
transitions.on: the treachery check, on its own clock
transitions.cost: orders quietly failing, and a flank you thought was held
transitions.explains: Not a betrayal you can point at. They are simply making sure you lose, which is cheaper and safer for them than switching sides and much harder to prove.

transitions.name: The banner turns
transitions.on: the treachery check, with the day going badly
transitions.cost: the contingent, and everything behind where it was standing
transitions.explains: Note that this needs the Tide against you as well as the treachery high. A traitor is a coward with arithmetic: he does not turn while you are winning. The counter to a treacherous vassal is therefore not to fix him — it is to not be losing.

transitions.name: You settle with them
transitions.on: amends, coin, a favour, or a grudge cooling
transitions.cost: whatever it took — and it is always cheaper than the alternative
transitions.explains: The number is a READING, not a stored score, so the moment the records behind it change, it changes. This is the arrow the whole court half of the game exists to let you fire.

transitions.name: The roads dry
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Into the campaigning season. Everything gets easier — and because everyone knows it, doing nothing now starts to cost you.

transitions.name: The fields come in
transitions.cost: an idle summer costs standing
transitions.explains: Into autumn. Food is everywhere and the army can feed itself off the country — and every farmer you call up now will remember it for years.

transitions.name: The cold comes
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Into winter. Marching is slow and exhausting and there is nothing to forage, so the granary drains fast. This is how armies starve without meeting anybody.

transitions.name: The year turns
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Round again — and with the service year, every vessel in the realm refills. The single most important date on the calendar, and the one a patient king plans his whole war around.

transitions.name: You name your cause
transitions.on: a proclamation going onto the record
transitions.cost: days at court
transitions.explains: The cause you choose sets your legitimacy, and legitimacy is the largest single term in whether anybody comes. A war of defence writes itself. A war of ambition you will pay for in favours, one house at a time.

transitions.name: The call goes out
transitions.on: a summons naming houses, a place and a day
transitions.cost: days at court, more for a whole realm
transitions.explains: Out of your hands and into theirs. Everything the court has been doing for years is about to be scored in a single reading.

transitions.name: The answers come back
transitions.cost: willingness, wherever a cup was dry
transitions.explains: No dice anywhere. Every answer is computed from loyalty, cause, season, grudges, distance and how much service is left in the cup — all of it visible beforehand if you looked. Whoever is missing, you can name the day you lost them.

transitions.name: Lords collect their men
transitions.cost: days, before a single league is walked
transitions.explains: Men have to come in off farms before anyone can march. A compact holding does it fast and a scattered one takes nearly twice as long, which is why land shape matters as much as land quantity.

transitions.name: They take the road
transitions.cost: fatigue, every day, all the way
transitions.explains: The long middle. Nothing dramatic happens and the battle is being decided anyway, one tired league at a time.

transitions.name: The host stands
transitions.cost: whatever the roads took
transitions.explains: Everyone who is coming has come. This is the moment the court half of the game is scored — and the army is always smaller than the one you imagined, because it always is.

transitions.name: The battle is fought
transitions.cost: men
transitions.explains: The host is handed to the battle engine with all its politics welded into its numbers — resolve, obedience, treachery, fatigue — and comes back as an aftermath.

transitions.name: It goes into the record
transitions.cost: none — and everything, later
transitions.explains: The dead, the taken, the deeds and the debts all become ACTS on the chronicle. Nothing is stored as a summary; every future reading recomputes itself from these records, which is why a battle keeps mattering for years.

transitions.name: You send them home
transitions.cost: every day already drawn from every vessel, and the goodwill
transitions.explains: One of the more expensive ways to do nothing. The men still lost the days, the cups still drained, and everyone involved formed an opinion about your judgement.

transitions.name: The first day is served
transitions.on: a house's men standing in your army for a day
transitions.cost: one day of the year's service
transitions.explains: The cup starts to empty. Nobody minds yet — this is exactly what the grant was for — but from here both of you are counting.

transitions.name: The cup runs out
transitions.on: the last owed day being served
transitions.cost: none, yet
transitions.explains: They owe you nothing more this year. Note what does NOT happen: no rule stops you calling them. The Vessel is not a fence, it is a price list.

transitions.name: You call them anyway
transitions.on: a summons to a dry house
transitions.cost: willingness now, and a grievance that compounds
transitions.explains: The decision the whole strategic layer turns on. Once is a favour asked. Twice is presumption. Three times and you have made an enemy of a man whose only fault was always turning up.

transitions.name: The service year turns
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Every cup in the realm fills again, used or not — so service you did not spend is service you lost. A king who understands this plans his wars around a date rather than around his temper.

transitions.name: They find out
transitions.cost: none — the cost starts now
transitions.explains: The clock starts HERE, not on the day you did it. A distant house can carry a brand-new grudge about something years old, and a secret injustice genuinely costs nothing right up until it does not.

transitions.name: It takes hold
transitions.on: the grievance being read at full weight
transitions.cost: willingness, resolve, obedience and treachery, all at once
transitions.explains: Now it is pulling on every number that decides whether an army turns up and does what it is told. One burning grievance is survivable. The trouble is that they are additive and you rarely have one.

transitions.name: It cools
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Time takes the heat out. This is the lazy king's strategy and it half works — it stops any single grudge from dominating, and it never clears the board.

transitions.name: It goes cold
transitions.cost: none
transitions.explains: Down to its residue and no further. Eleven cold grievances make an army that does not quite work and gives you nothing to point at — which is how most bad reigns actually feel from the inside.

transitions.name: You make it right
transitions.on: an act of amends going onto the record
transitions.cost: coin, land, a judgement, or your pride in public
transitions.explains: The real fix, and note how it works: the grudge is not deleted. The record of your amends is read ALONGSIDE the record of the wrong, which is both more honest and more durable than pretending it never happened.

transitions.name: The son takes it up
transitions.cost: a share of the weight, carried by someone new
transitions.explains: Outliving your enemies does not work. A long reign quietly accumulates dislike from people who were children when you earned it — so make amends while the man who was wronged is alive to accept them.

transitions.name: A price is named
transitions.cost: none to the captor
transitions.explains: Scaled to the man's standing, with a due date fixed the moment he was taken. A great lord is a windfall; a levy sergeant is barely worth the rope.

transitions.name: The ransom is paid
transitions.cost: coin — a great deal of it
transitions.explains: He rides home. If you paid for your own man, he and his whole house remember it: this is one of the cheapest ways to buy real loyalty in the game, and it is never cheap.

transitions.name: The date passes
transitions.cost: the realm's opinion, daily
transitions.explains: Nothing dramatic happens and everyone notices. A house watching its lord sit in another man's hall while its king does nothing is a house doing arithmetic about next season.

transitions.name: You pay late
transitions.cost: coin, and some of the credit you would have had
transitions.explains: Better than never by a wide margin. You get the man back and you do not get the gratitude you would have had for paying on time.

transitions.name: You leave him
transitions.cost: one of the deepest grudges available, spread to everyone watching
transitions.explains: Whatever you saved in coin you have spent several times over. Do this once and watch what the next muster looks like — not just from his house, from everyone who imagined themselves in his position.

transitions.name: He dies in captivity
transitions.cost: no ransom to anyone, and an heir with a grudge
transitions.explains: Nobody gets paid. The house inherits, the heir inherits a share of the grievance, and if the ransom was overdue when it happened, everyone will draw their own conclusions about whose fault that was.

transitions.name: You invest someone
transitions.on: an investiture going onto the record
transitions.cost: days at court, a stipend, and every rival's opinion
transitions.explains: The seat starts working — scaled by how much the holder likes you, so a brilliant officer who resents you is worth less than a competent one who does not. Everyone who wanted it and did not get it now has a number against your name.

transitions.name: It becomes customary
transitions.cost: nothing today; a great deal if you ever want it back
transitions.explains: No message, no ceremony, nothing to react to — the price of a decision you have not made yet quietly goes up. The most easily missed clock in the game.

transitions.name: His son expects it
transitions.cost: nothing today; ruinous later
transitions.explains: The family now considers it theirs by right. You can still take it back, and it will be one of the most expensive things you ever do.

transitions.name: You take it back
transitions.cost: a grievance scaled by how established he had become — and from an hereditary seat, fear in every other house
transitions.explains: Free from a fresh appointment and catastrophic from an established one. Stripping an hereditary office tells every other house exactly what their own grants are worth, and they will all price you accordingly.

transitions.name: The chair stands empty
transitions.cost: the seat's whole effect, until you fill it
transitions.explains: And now nobody is doing the job. A vacant Marshalcy means you direct two contingents at a time — so the gap between taking a seat back and filling it is a real and often badly-judged risk.

transitions.name: The holder dies
transitions.cost: the seat's effect, immediately
transitions.explains: The one way a seat empties with no grievance attached. A long-held seat falling vacant by death is an opportunity and a trap: the family expects the son, and they will notice what you do next.
